Vitamin B12 deficiency can result from inadequate dietary intake of Cbl, lack of IF, impaired intestinal absorption of IF-Cbl, or absence of vitamin B12 transport protein.
A liberal and varied diet should be supplemented with 50-300 mg/day of niacin; in severe cases or in patients with poor intestinal absorption, 100 mg may be given IV.
Gastrointestinal infections can precipitate clinical protein-energy malnutrition because of associated diarrhoea, anorexia, vomiting, increased metabolic needs, and decreased intestinal absorption.
PTH raises calcium by increasing bone resorption, renal calcium reabsorption and 1α-hydroxylation of vitamin D (more intestinal absorption), and it lowers phosphate by increasing its excretion.
Intestinal Absorption: Through its effect on vitamin D, PTH indirectly increases calcium absorption from the gastrointestinal tract.

qs.q: How does parathyroid hormone indirectly increase intestinal absorption of calcium?
o: Decreasing phosphate excretion in the renal tubules
Inhibiting calcitonin release from the thyroid
Promoting renal 1-alpha hydroxylation of vitamin D
Directly stimulating gut epithelial calcium pumps
qs.e: PTH does not directly act on the gut, but instead stimulates renal 1-alpha hydroxylase to activate vitamin D into calcitriol. Calcitriol then directly increases intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption.

qs.q: Which statement is false about impaired intestinal absorption? ---
o: Bile salt malabsorption occurs after terminal ileum removal
Iodide deficiency reduces thyroid size (It causes enlargement , i.e., goiter.)
Water absorption decreases in infants unable to digest disaccharides
Iron absorption decreases after stomach removal
qs.e: Iodide deficiency causes thyroid enlargement (goiter) due to TSH stimulation, not reduction in size.

ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: Intestinal absorption is the process by which nutrients and electrolytes cross the gut epithelium into circulation. It relies on active transport, facilitated diffusion, and paracellular pathways, all regulated by hormones and local factors. Clinicians must assess absorption defects to diagnose malnutrition, infections, and metabolic disorders.

sections.p: The small intestine is the main site for absorption of macronutrients, micronutrients, and water. The mucosal surface is maximised by villi and microvilli, and transporters on enterocytes mediate selective uptake.
b: Enterocytes are the main absorptive cells

sections.p: Nutrients enter cells via active transport (e.g., sodium‑glucose cotransport), facilitated diffusion (e.g., glucose via GLUT2), or passive paracellular flow. Water follows osmotic gradients.
b: Paracellular pores allow ions and water

t.b: Assess for hypokalemia or hyponatremia indicating malabsorption or diarrhea; high levels suggest renal loss or over‑replacement
Detect steatorrhea; high fat indicates pancreatic insufficiency or bile acid deficiency
Evaluate proximal small bowel function; low absorption suggests villous atrophy or celiac disease

sections.p: Hormones such as PTH and vitamin D enhance calcium absorption; gastrin and secretin influence fluid secretion; local cytokines modulate transporter expression.

sections.p: Common causes of impaired absorption include celiac disease, tropical sprue, Crohn’s disease, bacterial overgrowth, pancreatic insufficiency, and drug effects.

Serum electrolytes may be normal early; fecal fat can be falsely low if diet is low in fat. Stool elastase may be normal in mild pancreatic insufficiency.

faq.q: What is the difference between active and passive absorption?
faq.a: Active transport uses energy and carriers; passive relies on concentration gradients.

faq.q: Why does vitamin D matter for calcium absorption?
faq.a: It upregulates calcium transporters in enterocytes, increasing intestinal uptake.
